analysis.investment_thesis: Aequs is a capital-intensive conglomerate burning cash across three unrelated verticals — aerospace, toys, and consumer goods — with no earnings, a forward P/E of 1,140x, and an accelerating FCF drain of -239 Cr in FY25. There is no "story" here that justifies the price.
key_strengths: Aerospace & Defense tailwinds in India offer a real long-term secular trend
High gross margin of 56% suggests pricing power in certain segments
Heavy CWIP of 395 Cr signals capacity build that could eventually generate returns
key_risks: Extreme valuation — Forward P/E of 1,140x and EV/EBITDA of 288x with negative net profits (-102 Cr FY25) is completely unjustifiable
Free cash flow collapsed to -239 Cr in FY25 with capex of -265 Cr; company is burning through capital at an accelerating pace
Revenue actually declined from 965 Cr (FY24) to 925 Cr (FY25) while EBITDA collapsed from 163 Cr to 57 Cr — the story is getting worse, not better
red_flags: No PEG ratio computable — company is loss-making three years running (-110, -14, -102 Cr)
EBITDA destruction: down 65% YoY from 163 Cr to 57 Cr while revenue fell
Debt/Equity of 1.08 with only 61 Cr cash against 785 Cr borrowings — tight financial position during a capex surge
Other Income swung from +44 Cr to -6 Cr, suggesting the FY24 profit improvement was not operational
Conglomerate structure across aerospace, toys, and cookware — Lynch's worst nightmare for a simple story
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aequs is what I'd call a "confused story" — and confused stories get confused valuations. When I walk into a company that makes aircraft parts AND toys AND cookware AND runs industrial clusters AND logistics, I start worrying. Each of those is a separate business with different customers, different margins, different cycles. The aerospace piece is genuinely exciting — India's defense manufacturing push is real, and a vertically integrated player in Belgaum could become a niche dominator. But the toys and consumer goods divisions are diluting the narrative and apparently dragging down the numbers. FY25 EBITDA of 57 Cr on 925 Cr revenue is a 6.2% EBITDA margin — that's not aerospace economics, that's assembly line economics.

The valuation is simply absurd by any metric I've used in 40 years. A forward P/E of 1,140x means the market is pricing in a massive earnings recovery that hasn't even begun to show up. FCF deteriorated from -175 Cr to -239 Cr year-over-year while the 395 Cr CWIP tells me they're still building. That capital build could eventually pay off if aerospace orders materialize — but the P/S of 10x and P/B of 12.85x already price in a best-case scenario with no margin of safety. Lynch's Rule #1: Never pay a ridiculous price for a great story. At INR 171 with 11,200 Cr market cap, you're paying a premium for a turnaround that hasn't turned.
